Senses.Explanation: The phrase names the difficult joints and tangled turns where a saying or exchange cannot be handled by a smooth verbal explanation. Emperor Go-Daigo uses it when sending Daito written questions about difficult points in old sayings. Yuanwu Keqin calls the hard-to-bite, hard-to-penetrate point in Fayan’s answer such a joint, and says Xuedou’s verse brings it into view. Xiatang Huiyuan praises a layman’s freshly cut line by asking with whom he discusses its difficult joints and turns. Huishan Jiexian warns that without command of the school’s distinctions, someone facing such turns will not know how to change the working of the encounter.

Senses.Explanation: Guanyin Bodhisattva is the responsive figure invoked in answers, ritual appeals, and comic sayings. Guanyin Bodhisattva is an invoked figure whom Chan masters make answer questions, enter and leave the weeds, buy a flatbread that becomes a steamed bun, and stand for responsive compassion. Muzhou gives the name as an answer about the student's own self; Yunmen and Yi'an put Guanyin into the flatbread-and-bun saying; Baiyu stages Guanyin entering and leaving the weeds; Weilin and Jiqi invoke the figure in hall addresses.

SearchAliases: arrival of the bodhisattva of compassion
Senses.Explanation: “Guanyin Bodhisattva has arrived” is an arrival proclamation recorded both as a direct answer and at the opening of enacted sermon scenes. Lingyin Yinwen raises and strikes his staff, announces Avalokitesvara on its head, and then lends the figure a murmured line. Weilin Daopei raises his staff and follows the same announcement by asking whether the presence is whole-body or throughout the body. Sanyi Mingyu announces the figure and immediately turns his whisk into a flute-playing gesture. Yuanwu Keqin, without an accompanying implement action, gives the complete phrase as his direct answer when a monk asks which is mind. The records thus preserve three sermon stagings and one stand-alone interview answer under the same arrival wording.
Senses.Note: Guanyin is the Chinese name represented by Avalokitesvara; ‘is here’ is an allowed idiomatic alternate for the recorded arrival proclamation.

Senses.Explanation: Inspect mind or look at mind. The compound is attested, but 257 hits are concentrated in the Record of the Source-Mirror, and the corpus does not give the action one uniform set of predicates. In the Daoxin–Niutou Farong encounter, Farong answers ‘inspecting mind’ when asked what he is doing; Daoxin asks, ‘Who is doing the inspecting, and what thing is mind?’ (觀是何人心是何物。), and Farong gives no answer. The Treatise on Breaking Appearances says, ‘Only inspecting mind, this one thing, gathers all things’ (唯觀心一法，總攝諸法), then asks, ‘How does inspecting mind count as understanding?’ (云何觀心稱之為了). Its reply distinguishes a clean mind and a soiled mind and later says, ‘Inspecting mind in this way may be called understanding’ (如是觀心可名為了). The Record of the Source-Mirror quotes a different direct formula: ‘Inspect mind as no mind; things do not dwell on things; my mind is itself empty; fault and fortune have no owner—this is called correct inspection’ (觀心無心。法不住法。我心自空。罪福無主。即是無心無數。名為正觀。). Other Chan witnesses criticize particular uses. The Yongzheng Emperor says that making silence final and ‘then devoting oneself to quietly inspecting mind’ is ‘escaping a pit and falling into a ditch’ (便務靜觀心，又所謂逃坑落塹). Layman Xuri says, ‘closing the eyes, vainly seek seeing; inspecting mind, mistakenly seek penetration’ (閉目妄求見，觀心誤覓通). Zhang Tingyu, Layman Chenghuai, writes that ‘holding mind and inspecting mind divide guest and host’ (持心觀心紛主客). Chaoding Yuxuan writes, ‘if inspecting mind here is clear, the undivided single flavor is itself alert’ (於此觀心若了了，混然一味自惺惺). These are text-drawn assertions and criticisms by different named voices; they do not supply a single imported category for the headword.

Senses.Note: Two occurrences in one work count as one work, and no philosophical object-theory is added.
